t.1.123.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Arjuna, however, applied the utmost effort to honoring his guru and the highest application to the science of weapons, and he became the favorite of Droṇa.
t.1.123.3: Then once, while Arjuna was eating, a wind blew, and by it the lamp that was burning there was blown out.
t.1.123.2: Droṇa, however, then summoned the cook and told him in private: “Food is never, by any means, to be given by you to Arjuna in the dark.”
t.1.123.4: Arjuna went on eating his food, and the hand of that splendid one did not stray from his mouth, owing to its constant habit of taking food. Judging this to be the effect of practice, the Pāṇḍava began to practice at night.
t.1.123.6: I shall strive to act in such a way that no other archer in the world will be equal to you; this truth I tell you.
t.1.123.5: Droṇa heard the twang of his bowstring against his palm, O Bhārata. Rising up, he approached him, embraced him, and said this:
t.1.123.7: Then Droṇa further taught Arjuna the art of battle, on chariots and on elephants, on horses and also on the ground.
t.1.123.8: Droṇa trained the Pāṇḍava in fighting with the mace, in the handling of the sword, in the lance, the dart and the spear, and in mixed combat.
t.1.123.9: Seeing that skill of his, kings and princes eager to learn the science of archery came together by the thousands.
t.1.123.10: Then, great king, Ekalavya, the son of Hiraṇyadhanus, king of the Niṣādas, came to Droṇa.
t.1.123.12: But he, the scorcher of foes, having clasped Droṇa's feet with his head, went into the forest, and there he made a Droṇa out of earth.
t.1.123.11: Thinking, “He is a Niṣāda,” he who knew dharma did not accept him as a pupil in archery, out of regard for them alone.
t.1.123.14: Endowed with supreme faith and with supreme application, he attained the utmost lightness of hand in releasing, taking up, and fitting the arrow to the bow.
t.1.123.13: Then, having adopted the highest conduct of service toward him as his teacher, he devoted himself to the practice of archery, holding to the strictest discipline.
t.1.123.15: Then one day, with Droṇa's permission, all the Kurus and Pāṇḍavas, crushers of their foes, set out in their chariots on a hunt.
t.1.123.16: There, O king, a certain man, by chance, taking up his gear and bringing along a dog, followed the Pāṇḍavas alone.
t.1.123.18: That dog, catching sight in the forest of the dark Naiṣādi, his limbs smeared with dirt and wearing a black antelope skin, stood near him, barking.
t.1.123.17: While they were roaming there, each intent on doing one task or another, the dog, wandering about in the forest, went astray and approached the Niṣāda.
t.1.123.20: But that dog, its mouth filled with arrows, came to the Pāṇḍavas; seeing it, the heroic Pāṇḍavas were struck with the greatest astonishment.
t.1.123.19: Then, showing his deftness with the weapon, he shot seven arrows into the mouth of that barking dog, as though all at once.
t.1.123.22: Then, searching for him, the Pāṇḍavas, O king, saw that forest-dweller in the forest, ceaselessly shooting arrows.
t.1.123.21: Then, having seen that supreme deftness and that skill in striking a target by sound alone, and having beheld him, they were abashed, and they praised him in every way.
t.1.123.23: And they did not then recognize him, whose appearance was so altered; so they questioned him, asking, "Who are you, sir, and whose son are you?"
t.1.123.24: O heroes, know me to be the son of Hiraṇyadhanus, lord of the Niṣādas, and a pupil of Droṇa who has toiled at the science of archery.
t.1.123.25: The Pāṇḍavas, having truly come to know who he was, returned, and they told Droṇa the whole wondrous matter just as it had happened.
t.1.123.26: But Arjuna, the son of Kuntī, O king, remembering Ekalavya, approached Droṇa in private and, out of affection, spoke these words.
t.1.123.27: Was it not I alone whom you, embracing me with affection, addressed with these words: 'No pupil of mine shall ever surpass you'?
t.1.123.29: Droṇa, having pondered that resolve for what seemed but a moment, took Savyasācin with him and went to the Naiṣādi.
t.1.123.28: Why then is there another pupil of yours, the son of the lord of the Niṣādas, who surpasses me and is mightier even than all the world?
t.1.123.30: He saw Ekalavya, his limbs smeared with dirt, his hair matted, clad in rags, bow in hand, ceaselessly shooting arrows.
t.1.123.31: But Ekalavya, seeing Droṇa approaching from nearby, went up to him, clasped his feet, and touched the ground with his head.
t.1.123.32: Then the son of the Niṣāda, having duly honored Droṇa and declared himself his disciple, stood before him with joined palms.
t.1.123.33: Then, O king, Droṇa spoke these words to Ekalavya: "If you are my pupil, let my fee be given at once."
t.1.123.34: Ekalavya, hearing that, was delighted and said this: "What shall I give, blessed one? Let my guru command me."
t.1.123.35: "For there is nothing I would not give to my guru, O best of those who know brahman." He said to him, "Let your right thumb be given to me."
t.1.123.36: But Ekalavya, having heard that cruel speech of Droṇa, keeping his own promise and ever devoted to truth,
t.1.123.37: With his face still cheerful and his mind still undismayed, he cut off his own thumb without hesitation and gave it to Droṇa.
t.1.123.38: Thereafter the son of the Niṣāda drew the bowstring with his fingers, but he was no longer as swift as he had been before, O lord of men.
t.1.123.39: Then Arjuna became glad at heart, his fever of anxiety gone, and Droṇa proved true to his word, for no other surpassed Arjuna.
t.1.123.40: Then, among the Kurus, Duryodhana and Bhīma, the two pupils of Droṇa, took up mace practice in particular.
t.1.123.41: Aśvatthāmā became superior to all in the secret lore of weapons, and likewise the twins, both of them, surpassed other men as swordsmen; Yudhiṣṭhira was the best of chariot-fighters, but Dhanaṃjaya excelled in everything.
t.1.123.42: Throughout the sea-girt earth the Pāṇḍava became renowned as the leader of the leaders of chariot-troops, for his intelligence, discipline, strength and zeal, and for his mastery of all weapons.
t.1.123.43: In weaponry and in devotion to his teacher Arjuna became pre-eminent; though the instruction in arms was the same for all, the valiant Arjuna, by his skill, became the one atiratha among all the princes.
t.1.123.44: The evil-minded Dhārtarāṣṭras could not bear Bhīmasena, who surpassed them in strength, and Dhanaṃjaya, who had mastered his learning, O lord of men.
t.1.123.46: Having placed on the top of a tree an artificial bird, a bhāsa made by craftsmen, without the princes knowing of it, he pointed it out to them as the target.
t.1.123.45: Having gathered together all of them, who were accomplished in every branch of learning, Droṇa, O bull among men, wished to test their knowledge of weapons.
t.1.123.47: Droṇa said: Quickly now, all of you, take up your bows in haste, and aiming at this vulture, stand with your arrows fixed to the string.
t.1.123.48: And at the very moment I give the word, let its head be struck off. I shall direct you one by one; do as I say, my sons.
t.1.123.49: Then the best of the Āṅgirasas first said to Yudhiṣṭhira, "Fix the arrow, O invincible one, and release it at the end of my words."
t.1.123.51: Then, after a moment, O bull of the Bharatas, Droṇa spoke these words to that delight of the Kurus, who stood with his bow drawn.
t.1.123.50: Then Yudhiṣṭhira, urged on by his teacher's words, was the first to take up the loud-twanging bow, and he stood aiming at the bird.
t.1.123.52: "Do you see this vulture perched on the top of the tree, O son of the best of men?" "I see it," Yudhiṣṭhira thus replied to the teacher.
t.1.123.53: After what seemed but a moment, Droṇa spoke to him again: "Now, do you see this tree, or me, or even your brothers?"
t.1.123.54: The son of Kuntī said to him again and again, "I see this tree, and you as well, and my brothers, and the bird."
t.1.123.55: Droṇa, as if displeased, said to him, "Step aside!" and rebuked him, saying, "This target cannot be pierced by you."
t.1.123.56: Then the greatly renowned one, wishing to know, questioned in the very same manner those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana and the others.
t.1.123.58: Then Droṇa, smiling, addressed Dhanaṃjaya: "Now you must strike; behold this target."
t.1.123.57: In the same way he questioned the other pupils, Bhīma and the rest, and also the kings born in other lands; and they all, saying “We see all of that,” were likewise rebuked.
t.1.123.59: Your arrow should be released here at the very moment of my word. Having drawn your bow, son, stand ready for a little while.
t.1.123.60: Thus addressed, Savyasācin, his bow drawn into a circle, stood aiming at the target, urged on by the words of his teacher.
t.1.123.61: After a moment, as it were, Droṇa spoke to him in the same way: "Do you see this bird perched there, the tree, or even me?"
t.1.123.63: Then the invincible Droṇa, his heart gladdened, after what seemed but a moment, spoke again to him, the bull among the chariot-warriors of the Pāṇḍavas.
t.1.123.62: "I see this bird," Pārtha said to Droṇa, O Bhārata, "but I do not see the tree or you."
t.1.123.64: "If you see this vulture, then tell me so again." He said, "I see the head of the vulture, not its body."
t.1.123.65: Addressed thus by Arjuna, Droṇa, his body hair bristling with delight, said to Pārtha, "Release it!" And he released it without hesitation.
t.1.123.66: Then, with a sharpened razor-edged arrow, the Pāṇḍava swiftly cut off the head of the bird perched on the tree and made it fall.
t.1.123.67: When that feat was accomplished, he embraced Phalguna, and he deemed Drupada already defeated in battle together with his kinsmen.
t.1.123.69: Then, as Droṇa was immersed in the water, a mighty crocodile dwelling in the water, impelled by fate, seized him at the end of his shank.
t.1.123.68: Then, after some time had passed, O bull of the Bharatas, the best of the Aṅgirases went with his disciples to the Gaṅgā to bathe.
t.1.123.70: Though he himself was capable of getting free, he urged all his pupils, as if hurrying them on: "Kill the crocodile and set me free!"
t.1.123.72: And seeing him endowed with diligent practice, Droṇa considered the Pāṇḍava superior to all his pupils, and he was then filled with delight.
t.1.123.71: At the very moment of his words, Bībhatsu struck the crocodile submerged in the water with five sharp arrows loosed in quick succession, while the others, utterly bewildered, ran here and there.
t.1.123.73: Cut into many pieces by the arrows of Pārtha, the crocodile let go of the great-souled one's leg and met its death.
t.1.123.74: Then Bhāradvāja said to the great-souled, great chariot-warrior: "Take, O mighty-armed one, this supreme and most irresistible weapon named Brahmaśiras, together with the means of its discharge and withdrawal."
t.1.123.75: And this must by no means be used by you against men; if it were hurled at one of little power, it would burn up the whole world.
t.1.123.76: This weapon, dear son, is said to be without equal in the worlds. You should bear it with self-restraint; and hear this word of mine.
t.1.123.77: O hero, should any non-human enemy ever oppress you, then you should employ this weapon in battle to slay him.
t.1.123.78: Promising "So be it," Bībhatsu, with joined palms, received that supreme weapon; and the teacher spoke to him again: "No other man in the world will be an archer equal to you."
